definition: Abstract thinking is the ability to work with concepts and general ideas rather than only concrete facts, supporting deeper conceptual understanding. In learning, it helps students connect knowledge across areas and turn understanding into innovative practice, especially when paired with inquiry skills and self-regulation.

reasons: The definition adds a general psychopedagogical meaning for abstract thinking (“ability to work with concepts and general ideas rather than only concrete facts”) that is not stated in the packet.
The claims about “deeper conceptual understanding” and about students connecting knowledge across areas are broader than the packet’s specific findings and wording.
The phrase “especially when paired with inquiry skills and self-regulation” overgeneralizes a study finding about one mediating model into a general definition.

The packet does not define “abstract thinking” as an ability to work with concepts/general ideas rather than concrete facts; it only references an “abstract thinking and conceptual understanding” construct (ATCU) in relation to other variables.

Claims about “supporting deeper conceptual understanding” and “connect knowledge across areas” are not explicitly stated as definitional attributes of abstract thinking in the packet; the packet instead reports statistical relationships among ATCU, IESR, and IIPI.

The definition’s claim that abstract thinking helps “turn understanding into innovative practice” is only indirectly supported via the reported finding that ATCU predicts interdisciplinary integration and practical innovation (IIPI), but the packet does not substantively define abstract thinking in these terms.

The phrase “especially when paired with inquiry skills and self-regulation” is only broadly supported by the mediating role of inquiry execution and strategic regulation (IESR); however, the packet does not present this as a general conditional statement about abstract thinking being “paired” with these skills.
